description: GeoVision Earth is a multidisciplinary team exploring Earth observation, remote sensing, GIS, and geospatial data science. With experience in hydrology, environmental analysis, and machine learning, we aim to transform satellite data into meaningful insights. We welcome passionate collaborators with skills in Python, SAR processing, data visualization, web development, and scientific communication to build innovative, impactful solutions.
summary:
GOVISION EARTH – SARFlow Explorer is an interactive geospatial application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge. The project explores surface-water changes in Prachin Buri, Thailand, using NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band SAR observations acquired on September 6, September 30, and October 12, 2026.

The application enables users to compare ascending and descending radar observations, examine their spatial agreement and differences, explore orbit-fusion strategies, and visualize changes through interactive maps, swipe comparisons, and temporal animation.

A reproducible geospatial workflow integrates radar processing, surface-water classification, contextual Earth observation datasets, and exploratory comparison with Sentinel-2 optical observations.

By translating complex SAR analyses into an accessible WebGIS platform, the project demonstrates how open satellite data can support environmental monitoring and spatial decision-making. Its mapped outputs represent potential surface-water conditions, not independently verified flood extents.
details:
Project Overview

GOVISION EARTH – SARFlow Explorer is an interactive geospatial application developed in response to the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Dancing with the SARs. The project examines how different radar viewing geometries influence the identification and spatial interpretation of potential surface-water conditions. The demonstration focuses on a geographic search area in Prachin Buri, Thailand, using NASA–ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) observations.

Data and Methodology

The analysis uses NISAR Level-2 Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance (GCOV) data acquired in ascending and descending orbital configurations on 6 September, 30 September, and 12 October 2026. HH and HV radar measurements were processed using Python within a common 10 m analysis grid referenced to UTM Zone 47N (EPSG:32647).

The workflow comprises observation and acquisition verification, SAR preprocessing, ancillary data preparation, independent ascending and descending analyses, surface-water candidate classification, orbit fusion, exploratory validation, and preliminary exposure assessment.

Two complementary orbit-fusion approaches were evaluated: the union of water candidates identified by either orbit (Fusion OR) and the intersection of candidates identified by both orbits (Fusion AND). Additional agreement and disagreement maps illustrate how radar viewing geometry influences the spatial distribution of detections.

Contextual information was obtained from NASA GPM IMERG precipitation, Copernicus Sentinel-2 imagery, JRC Global Surface Water, and ESA WorldCover 2021.

Interactive Application

The analytical results were integrated into a browser-based WebGIS developed with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Leaflet. Users can examine three observation dates, select ascending or descending radar perspectives, compare orbit-fusion strategies, adjust thematic-layer opacity, and explore spatial differences using side-by-side maps, a swipe comparison tool, and temporal animation.

The application presents geospatial observations alongside quantitative area summaries, allowing users to investigate both the spatial extent and the temporal behavior of radar-derived water candidates.

Results and Evaluation

On 30 September 2026, approximately 359.67 km² were identified as potential surface water by both radar viewing geometries.

An exploratory comparison was conducted using automated, single-scene Sentinel-2 optical reference labels. Of 260 sampled locations, 162 met the optical screening criteria across 51 spatial blocks.

Within this sample, the F1 scores were 0.754 for Ascending, 0.802 for Descending, 0.556 for Fusion AND, and 0.930 for Fusion OR.

These scores describe agreement with an automatically generated optical reference. They do not represent independent field-validated flood-mapping accuracy or area-wide classification accuracy.

A preliminary spatial overlay also identified approximately 259.05 km² where shared radar-derived water candidates intersected areas mapped as cropland in ESA WorldCover 2021. This intersection is not a measure of actual crop damage or economic loss.

Contribution and Potential Applications

The principal contribution of GOVISION EARTH is the integration of multiple NISAR radar perspectives, temporal observations, and transparent classification comparisons within an accessible interactive mapping environment.

Rather than presenting a single classification as definitive, the platform enables users to examine agreement, disagreement, and uncertainty between radar observations. This approach supports scientific communication, geospatial education, environmental monitoring, and the exploratory assessment of changing surface-water conditions.

Limitations and Reproducibility

The analysis has several important limitations. The first observation is a prior satellite acquisition rather than an independently verified dry baseline. Ascending and descending acquisitions are separated by approximately 11 hours, and radar backscatter can be influenced by wet soil, agricultural conditions, and other surface characteristics.

Independent georeferenced flood-reference polygons were unavailable for the study area. Accordingly, the resulting maps should not be interpreted as confirmed flood boundaries or operational flood warnings.

The application, supporting documentation, and web-development source code are available at:

https://github.com/MohamedTammam-Geo/govision-earth

Interactive application:

https://mohamedtammam-geo.github.io/govision-earth/
